A patent is a statutory right granted for an invention that meets the requirements of patentability under applicable law. In India, a patent can protect a new product or process involving an inventive step and capable of industrial application.

Novelty: The invention must be new and not already publicly disclosed.

Patentable Subject Matter: The invention must not fall within the exclusions under the Patents Act, 1970.

A Section 8 Company is a not-for-profit company registered under the Companies Act, 2013, for objectives such as education, social welfare, science, art, environmental protection, and other charitable purposes. When such a company is no longer required or meets the applicable conditions for closure, its name may be removed from the Register of Companies through the prescribed strike-off process.
A Section 8 Company may be considered for strike off in circumstances such as:
Voluntary Closure: The company is no longer carrying on activities or has fulfilled its objectives.
Non-Compliance: Failure to comply with applicable filing and statutory requirements may lead to regulatory action.
Inactivity: The company has remained inactive and meets the conditions prescribed for removal of its name.
Regulatory Non-Compliance: Breach of applicable requirements or conditions governing the company may result in regulatory action.
Other Legal or Regulatory Grounds: The Registrar or competent authority may initiate proceedings where permitted under applicable law.
Strike off is governed primarily by Section 248 of the Companies Act, 2013 and the applicable rules.
Where eligible, the company may apply for removal of its name by:
Board Approval: Directors approve the proposal for strike off.
Members’ Approval: The required members' resolution and approvals are obtained.
Settlement of Liabilities: Applicable liabilities and statutory obligations are addressed before filing.
Filing Form STK-2: The prescribed application is submitted to the ROC along with required documents, declarations, and supporting records.
ROC Review and Notice: The ROC examines the application and follows the prescribed notice and publication process before passing the final order.
The Registrar of Companies (ROC) may initiate removal proceedings where the company falls within the circumstances prescribed under Section 248.
Issuance of notice to the company and its directors.
Opportunity to submit an explanation or representation.
Removal of the company's name from the Register of Companies if the requirements are satisfied.
Once the company is struck off:
The company generally ceases to operate as a registered company, subject to statutory provisions.
Its ability to carry on business and undertake transactions is restricted.
Directors and officers may remain liable for obligations arising under applicable law, and disqualification can arise in specified circumstances.
Outstanding legal proceedings may continue where permitted by law.
Assets and liabilities are dealt with in accordance with the Companies Act and applicable rules.

Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) may be required to file an income tax return in India for income that is taxable in India. Their tax liability depends on residential status, the source and nature of income, applicable deductions, and any relief available under a Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA).

Residential status is determined under the Income Tax Act, 1961, primarily based on the individual's stay in India during the relevant financial year and, in certain cases, their stay during preceding years and other statutory conditions.
An individual who does not qualify as a resident under the applicable rules is generally treated as a non-resident (NRI) for Indian income-tax purposes.
NRIs are generally taxed in India on income that is received, accrued, or deemed to be received or accrue in India, subject to applicable provisions. Common sources include:
Salary Income: Salary for services performed in India is generally taxable in India, subject to applicable rules.
Rental Income: Rent from property in India is taxable. Eligible deductions, including the applicable standard deduction and municipal taxes, may be claimed subject to the law.
Capital Gains: Gains from the sale of Indian property, shares, securities, or mutual funds may be taxable. The applicable treatment depends on the asset, holding period, and relevant tax provisions.

Interest Income: Interest from Indian bank accounts and deposits may be taxable. Interest on eligible NRE accounts is generally exempt subject to applicable conditions, while NRO interest is generally taxable.
Other Income: Business income, professional income, dividends, and other India-linked income may also be taxable.

NRIs are generally subject to the income-tax rates applicable to individuals, but the applicable regime, slab rates, special rates, surcharge, cess, and other provisions depend on the relevant financial year and nature of income.

Section 80C: Eligible investments and payments such as life insurance premiums, EPF contributions, and eligible home-loan principal repayment.
Section 80D: Eligible health insurance premiums, subject to applicable conditions.

DTAA Relief: NRIs may claim relief under an applicable Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement where the same income is taxable in India and another country, subject to the treaty and prescribed conditions.
Other Applicable Benefits: Certain deductions, exemptions, and allowances may be available depending on the nature of income and the applicable tax regime.

NRIs should determine their residential status and taxable Indian income before selecting the appropriate ITR form. The return should include relevant Indian income, eligible deductions, taxes paid or deducted at source, and applicable foreign/treaty information where required.

Goods and Services Tax (GST) is an indirect tax on the supply of goods and services in India. It replaced several earlier indirect taxes and provides a common framework for taxation across the country. GST also enables eligible businesses to claim Input Tax Credit (ITC), subject to applicable conditions.
Multi-Stage Tax: GST applies at different stages of the supply chain, with credit available for eligible taxes paid.

Multiple Tax Rates: Different goods and services are subject to different GST rates as prescribed by law.
Dual GST Structure: CGST and SGST/UTGST generally apply to intra-state supplies, while IGST applies to inter-state supplies.
Input Tax Credit: Eligible businesses can claim credit for GST paid on purchases, subject to prescribed conditions.

Businesses must obtain GST registration when they cross the applicable turnover threshold or fall under a category requiring compulsory registration. Thresholds and exemptions vary based on the nature of supply, state, and other applicable conditions.
Return Filing: Taxpayers must file applicable GST returns and statements according to their registration and scheme.
E-Invoicing: E-invoicing applies to specified taxpayers meeting the prescribed turnover and other conditions.
GST Payments: Tax liabilities are generally paid electronically through the GST system.
Reconciliation: Businesses should regularly reconcile books, invoices, returns, and ITC to identify discrepancies.
Return Filing: Managing multiple reporting requirements and deadlines.

Greater Transparency: Digital reporting and documentation improve transaction visibility.

GST-registered businesses are required to file applicable returns or statements with the tax authorities. GST returns generally contain details of outward supplies, tax liability, and eligible input tax credit. Timely and accurate filing helps businesses maintain compliance and claim eligible ITC.
The applicable GST form depends on the taxpayer’s registration type and activities. Key forms include:
GSTR-1 – Reports details of outward supplies of goods and services by regular taxpayers.
GSTR-3B – Summary return used by applicable taxpayers to declare tax liability and claim eligible input tax credit.
GSTR-4 – Annual return applicable to taxpayers under the composition scheme, subject to applicable rules.
GSTR-5 – Return for non-resident taxable persons.
GSTR-6 – Return for Input Service Distributors.
GSTR-7 – Return for persons required to deduct TDS under GST.
GSTR-8 – Statement filed by e-commerce operators required to collect TCS.
GSTR-9 – Annual return for applicable taxpayers.
GSTR-10 – Final return after cancellation or surrender of GST registration.
GSTR-11 – Statement for persons holding a Unique Identity Number (UIN) seeking refunds.
GSTR-2A is an auto-drafted statement of inward supplies, rather than a return that the taxpayer files.
Login to the GST Portal – Access the official GST portal and log in with your credentials.
Select the Applicable Return – Choose the relevant return and filing period.
Enter Transaction Details – Report outward supplies, tax liability, and eligible ITC as applicable.
Reconcile Records – Match return data with invoices, books, and available GST records.
Pay Tax Liability – Pay any balance tax liability after adjusting eligible credits.
File the Return – Verify and file the return using the applicable authentication method, such as DSC or EVC.
Save the Acknowledgment – Keep the filed return and ARN for future reference.

Late or incorrect GST return filing can result in late fees, interest, notices, and other consequences under applicable GST provisions. Continued non-compliance may also affect the taxpayer's GST compliance status and can lead to further action by the authorities.
The exact late fee and interest depend on the type of return, tax liability, period of delay, and applicable provisions, so fixed amounts should not be stated universally.

Every business registered in India must comply with the regulations set by the Registrar of Companies (ROC) under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA). To manage these complexities, businesses often seek professional assistance from an ROC Filing Consultant. These consultants help companies navigate compliance requirements efficiently, reducing legal risks and penalties.
An ROC Filing Consultant is responsible for assisting businesses in filing mandatory returns and documents within the prescribed time. Their key responsibilities include:
Company Registration Support: Helping businesses register under the Companies Act, 2013, and ensuring compliance with initial documentation.
Annual ROC Filings: Assisting in filing Annual Returns (MGT-7)and Financial Statements (AOC-4) with the ROC.
Event-Based Filings: Ensuring timely submission of forms for changes in the company’s structure, such as directorship modifications, share allotments, and capital alterations.
Compliance Advisory: Providing guidance on corporate governance, statutory requirements, and best practices.

Maintaining Statutory Registers: Keeping updated records as per legal norms, including registers of members, charges, and directors.
Liaison with Authorities: Communicating with the ROC and MCA on behalf of the company for smooth compliance.

Maintaining Transparency: Proper filing ensures transparency in financial matters.
Enhancing Business Credibility: A compliant company gains trust among investors and stakeholders.
Ensuring Business Continuity: Timely filings prevent legal disruptions that can impact business operations.

Starting a business involves choosing the right legal structure, completing applicable registrations, and meeting regulatory requirements. In India, eligible businesses can also apply for DPIIT Startup Recognition to access certain government benefits and support.
Startup registration generally involves establishing a business as a company, LLP, or other suitable entity and, where eligible, obtaining recognition under the DPIIT Startup India initiative.

DPIIT recognition is separate from basic business incorporation and may provide eligible startups access to certain tax benefits, intellectual property support, funding programs, and regulatory benefits.

Funding Opportunities: Eligible startups may access government-backed funding programs and other financing opportunities.

Business Credibility: Formal registration can strengthen credibility with customers, investors, and partners.

Sole Proprietorship – Simple structure owned and operated by one individual, but without separate legal identity.
Partnership – Two or more persons share ownership and responsibilities under a partnership arrangement.
LLP – Combines partnership flexibility with limited liability and separate legal identity.
Private Limited Company – Separate legal entity with limited liability and a structure suitable for raising investment.
Public Limited Company – Generally suited to larger businesses seeking to raise capital from the public.

A sole proprietorship is one of the simplest forms of business ownership. It is owned and operated by a single individual, with fewer formalities and relatively simple compliance requirements. This guide covers the key aspects of setting up a sole proprietorship, along with its advantages and limitations.

A sole proprietorship is a business owned and managed by one individual. The proprietor is personally responsible for the business’s debts and liabilities. Unlike a company or LLP, it does not have a separate legal identity from its owner. In India, there is no single central registration for a sole proprietorship; applicable registrations depend on the nature and location of the business.

PAN and Tax Compliance:The proprietor generally uses their individual PAN for income-tax purposes and must comply with applicable tax requirements.

Maintain Business Records:Keep proper records of income, expenses, invoices, and other transactions, along with applicable tax and statutory filings.
Ensure Ongoing Compliance:Renew applicable licences and comply with tax, labour, municipal, and industry-specific regulations.
Easy Formation: Fewer formalities and relatively low setup costs.
Full Control: The proprietor has complete control over business decisions.

Partnership registration provides a formal structure for individuals who want to establish and operate a business together. A partnership is a business arrangement in which two or more individuals agree to share profits, responsibilities, and business activities. While registration requirements may vary depending on the jurisdiction, registering a partnership can provide greater legal clarity and help establish clear rights and responsibilities among the partners.

A partnership is formed through an agreement between two or more individuals who agree to carry on a business and share its profits. The terms of the relationship between the partners are generally documented through a Partnership Deed, which sets out their respective rights, duties, contributions, and profit-sharing arrangements.
A properly drafted partnership agreement can help reduce misunderstandings and provide a clear framework for managing the business and resolving potential disputes.
A partnership generally has the following features:
1. Agreement Between PartnersA partnership arises from an agreement between the partners. The Partnership Deed forms the basis of the relationship and defines the terms governing the business.
2. Two or More PersonsA partnership requires at least two individuals who agree to carry on a business together and share its profits.
3. Sharing of ProfitsThe partners agree on how the profits and losses of the business will be shared, usually as specified in the Partnership Deed.
4. Business MotiveA partnership is generally established to carry on a business or commercial activity with the objective of earning profits.

5. Mutual AgencyEach partner can act as an agent of the partnership in relation to the business. Acts performed by one partner within the scope of the partnership can bind the firm and the other partners.
6. Unlimited LiabilityIn a traditional partnership, the liability of partners is generally unlimited, meaning partners may be personally liable for the firm's obligations, subject to applicable law.
Registering a partnership can provide several practical and legal advantages:
1. Legal RecognitionA registered partnership can provide greater formal recognition and credibility when dealing with customers, suppliers, financial institutions, and other business stakeholders.
2. Clear Terms and ConditionsA properly drafted Partnership Deed clearly defines the roles, responsibilities, capital contributions, and profit-sharing arrangements of the partners.
3. Dispute ResolutionClearly documented partnership terms can help provide a framework for addressing disagreements and resolving disputes between partners.
4. Tax and Financial ComplianceA registered partnership can complete applicable tax registrations and comply with relevant tax requirements based on its business activities and applicable laws.
5. Ease of Business OperationsA formal partnership structure can make it easier to open a business bank account, enter into contracts, obtain financing, and manage business transactions.

The exact registration process varies depending on the applicable state and jurisdiction. In India, a partnership firm is generally registered with the relevant Registrar of Firms under the applicable state Partnership Act provisions.

The partners should select a suitable business name that complies with applicable legal requirements. The name should not conflict with an existing business or contain restricted words where prohibited.
The Partnership Deed is an important document that establishes the terms of the partnership. It may include:
Names and addresses of all partners
Rules for admission or retirement of partners
Terms relating to dissolution of the partnership

The Partnership Deed should be executed on the appropriate stamp paper and signed by all partners in accordance with the applicable state requirements. Notarization may be required depending on the applicable procedure.

The partners must submit the prescribed application and supporting documents to the relevant Registrar of Firms. Documents may include the Partnership Deed, identity and address proofs of partners, registered office proof, and other prescribed forms.

After verification and approval of the application, the Registrar of Firms records the partnership in the applicable register and issues the relevant registration confirmation or certificate, as prescribed by the respective state.
After registration, the partnership should continue to meet applicable legal, tax, and business requirements, which may include:
Tax Registration – Obtain PAN and GST registration where applicable.
Business Licenses – Obtain industry-specific licenses or registrations where required.
Bank Account Opening – Open a dedicated business bank account in the partnership firm's name.
Tax Filing – File applicable income tax and other returns within the prescribed timelines.
Maintain Financial Records – Maintain proper books of account and supporting financial records.
Update Partnership Details – Report applicable changes in partners, business address, or other firm details to the relevant authorities.

India is a growing business destination for foreign companies seeking to expand their operations and access the Indian market. Foreign businesses can establish a presence in India through different legal structures, depending on their business objectives, investment requirements, and applicable regulatory conditions. Understanding the available options, incorporation process, and ongoing compliance requirements is essential before establishing a business presence in India.
Foreign companies can establish their presence in India through the following structures:

A foreign company can establish a wholly owned subsidiary in India by incorporating a private limited company under the Companies Act, 2013. This structure may be suitable where 100% Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is permitted in the relevant sector, subject to applicable conditions.

A foreign company can enter into a joint venture with an Indian company or investor. This structure allows the parties to share ownership, resources, expertise, and business responsibilities, subject to applicable FDI and regulatory requirements.

A liaison office can be established to represent the foreign parent company, explore business opportunities, facilitate communication, and promote its interests in India. A liaison office generally cannot undertake commercial activities or earn income in India.

A branch office is an extension of the foreign company and may undertake permitted activities such as export and import, consultancy, research, and other activities approved under applicable regulations. Its activities are subject to the conditions prescribed by the relevant authorities.

A foreign company may establish a project office in India for executing a specific project or contract. This structure can be suitable for foreign businesses involved in construction, infrastructure, engineering, and other project-based activities.
The incorporation process generally involves the following steps:
Determine the appropriate structure based on the nature of the proposed business, ownership requirements, investment plans, and applicable FDI and regulatory provisions.

Where required, the proposed directors must obtain a Digital Signature Certificate (DSC) and Director Identification Number (DIN) for completing electronic filings with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA).
Select a suitable name and apply for name reservation through the applicable MCA process. The proposed name must comply with the prescribed naming guidelines.

Prepare the required incorporation documents, which may include the Memorandum of Association (MoA), Articles of Association (AoA), identity and address documents, declarations, and documents relating to the foreign parent company.

For an Indian subsidiary, the applicable incorporation forms, including SPICe+, are submitted electronically to the Registrar of Companies (RoC), along with the required documents and prescribed fees.
After the application is reviewed and approved, the RoC issues the Certificate of Incorporation, confirming the legal existence of the Indian company.
After incorporation, the company may need to obtain PAN and TAN, complete applicable GST registration, open a business bank account, and meet other tax and regulatory requirements.

Foreign companies establishing a presence in India must comply with applicable provisions of the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) regulations, FDI policies, the Companies Act, tax laws, and sector-specific regulations.

Depending on the structure and nature of operations, compliance obligations may include maintaining proper financial records, filing applicable returns and financial statements, meeting tax requirements, reporting foreign investments, and submitting prescribed filings to the relevant authorities.

Registering a Producer Company provides farmers, agriculturists, and other primary producers with a formal business structure to improve their collective growth and financial opportunities. Governed by the Companies Act, 2013, a Producer Company helps members strengthen their market access, bargaining power, and business operations. Understanding the registration process, eligibility requirements, and benefits is essential before establishing a Producer Company in India.

A Producer Company is a legally recognized entity formed by primary producers to promote activities such as production, harvesting, procurement, grading, processing, marketing, selling, and exporting agricultural or other primary produce. Its primary objective is to improve the economic well-being of its members through collective business activities.
A Producer Company offers several important features:
1. Minimum Membership: A Producer Company can be formed by ten or more individual producers, two or more producer institutions, or a combination permitted under applicable law.
2. No Maximum Membership Limit: There is generally no upper limit on the number of members.
3. Limited Liability: Members' liability is generally limited to their shareholding, subject to applicable laws.
4. Separate Legal Entity: The company has a legal identity separate from its members and can own assets and enter into contracts in its own name.
5. Perpetual Succession: The company continues to exist even when its members change.
6. Producer-Based Membership: Membership and shareholding are subject to the eligibility requirements prescribed for Producer Companies.
Registering a Producer Company can provide several advantages:
Better Market Opportunities: Collective production and marketing can help reduce costs and improve market access.
Access to Government Schemes: Eligible Producer Companies may benefit from applicable government schemes, subsidies, and financial assistance.
Financial Assistance: Registration can help establish credibility when approaching banks and financial institutions for business financing.
Tax Benefits: Certain agricultural activities may qualify for tax exemptions, subject to applicable tax laws.
Professional Management: A Board of Directors provides a structured framework for managing business operations and decision-making.
The registration process generally involves the following steps:
Proposed directors and other required signatories must obtain DSCs to digitally sign the incorporation documents.
The proposed directors must obtain valid DINs through the applicable Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) process.

Choose a unique name and submit it for approval through the applicable MCA name reservation process. The name must comply with the prescribed naming guidelines and include the words “Producer Company Limited.”

Prepare the Memorandum of Association (MoA), Articles of Association (AoA), identity and address proofs, registered office documents, and other prescribed declarations. Submit the incorporation application through the MCA portal.
After verification and approval, the Registrar of Companies issues the Certificate of Incorporation, confirming the company's legal existence.

A Nidhi Company is a type of Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) that operates in India with the primary objective of cultivating the habit of savings and thrift among its members. Registered under Section 406 of the Companies Act, 2013, a Nidhi Company is governed by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) and follows the Nidhi Rules, 2014. Unlike other NBFCs, a Nidhi Company is restricted to accepting deposits and lending money to its members, making it a unique financial institution.
Member-Centric Operations: A Nidhi Company can only deal with its members, meaning it cannot engage with external individuals or institutions.
Encourages Savings: The company fosters the habit of savings among its members, which promotes financial discipline.
Limited Liability: The liability of members is limited, protecting them from financial risks beyond their contributions.
No External Involvement: It cannot engage in chit funds, hire-purchase, leasing, or insurance businesses.
Regulated by MCA: Though it falls under the NBFC category, it is exempt from Reserve Bank of India (RBI) oversight, reducing regulatory burdens.
To register a Nidhi Company in India, certain eligibility criteria must be met:
Minimum Members: A minimum of seven members is required to start the company, with at least three acting as directors.
Capital Requirement: A minimum paid-up equity share capital of Rs. 5 lakh is necessary.
Unique Name: The company’s name must include the word “Nidhi Limited.”
No Preference Shares: A Nidhi Company cannot issue preference shares.
Obtain Digital Signature Certificate (DSC): Directors must have DSCs for online registration.
Director Identification Number (DIN): All directors need a DIN issued by the MCA.
Reserve a Name: The company’s name must be unique and should be approved by the MCA.
Draft Memorandum and Articles of Association: These legal documents define the company’s objectives and operational framework.
File Incorporation Application: The final application is submitted to the MCA along with required documents and fees.
Obtain Certificate of Incorporation: Once approved, the company is legally recognized as a Nidhi Company.
Membership: A Nidhi Company must have at least 200 members within one year of incorporation.
Net-Owned Funds (NOF): The ratio of Net Owned Funds to deposits should be 1:20.
Loan Limits: The company can provide secured loans only against gold, property, or fixed deposits.
Branch Expansion: A Nidhi Company can open branches only after three years of successful operations and within the same state.
Interest Rate Cap: The maximum interest rate on loans cannot exceed 7.5% above the highest rate offered on deposits.
Simple Formation Process: Less regulatory scrutiny compared to other NBFCs.
Limited Compliance Burden: No RBI intervention in daily operations.
Encourages Community Development: Facilitates small-scale savings and lending for financial inclusion.

Limited Liability: The member’s liability is generally limited to the extent of their shareholding, subject to applicable law.
Separate Legal Entity: The OPC has a legal identity separate from its member.
Perpetual Succession: A nominee is appointed to take over membership in the event of the member’s death.
Simplified Compliance: OPCs generally have fewer compliance requirements than private limited companies.
Single Member: Only one individual can incorporate an OPC.

Nominee: A nominee must be appointed as prescribed under the Companies Act.

A Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) combines the flexibility of a partnership with the benefit of limited liability. It is a suitable business structure for entrepreneurs, professionals, and small businesses seeking a separate legal entity with flexible management and comparatively simpler compliance requirements.

An LLP is a separate legal entity from its partners, providing limited liability protection to them, subject to applicable laws. In India, LLPs are governed by the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008. An LLP can own property, enter into contracts, and conduct business in its own name.
Limited Liability Protection: Partners’ personal assets are generally protected from business liabilities.
Separate Legal Entity: The LLP has an identity separate from its partners.
Flexible Management: Partners can structure the business and responsibilities through the LLP Agreement.
No Minimum Capital Requirement: An LLP can be incorporated with the capital agreed upon by the partners.
Simpler Compliance: LLPs generally have fewer statutory requirements than companies, subject to applicable laws.
Perpetual Succession: The LLP continues to exist despite changes in its partners.
Flexible Ownership: Partners can be admitted or their interests changed in accordance with the LLP Agreement and applicable law.
Minimum Two Partners: At least two partners are required, including designated partners.
Resident Designated Partner: At least one designated partner must satisfy the applicable Indian residency requirement.
Unique Name: The proposed name must comply with MCA naming rules and should not conflict with existing entities or trademarks.
Registered Office: A valid registered office address in India is required.
DSC and DIN/DPIN: Designated partners must meet the applicable digital signature and identification requirements.
Obtain DSC: Designated partners require Digital Signature Certificates for electronic filing.
Obtain DIN/DPIN: The applicable director identification number is obtained for designated partners.
Reserve the LLP Name: Apply for name reservation through the MCA portal.
File Incorporation Application: Submit Form FiLLiP with the required documents and registered office details.
File LLP Agreement: The agreement defines the rights, duties, contributions, and responsibilities of the partners and must be filed within the prescribed period.
Receive Certificate of Incorporation: Upon approval, the Registrar issues the Certificate of Incorporation and LLP Identification Number (LLPIN).
Obtain PAN/TAN and Open Bank Account: Complete applicable tax registrations and open a bank account in the LLP’s name.
Form 11: Annual Return of the LLP.
Form 8: Statement of Account and Solvency.
Income Tax Return: Annual income-tax filing as applicable.
Audit: Required when the LLP crosses the applicable turnover or contribution threshold.

Failure to meet LLP compliance requirements can result in additional fees, penalties, and other legal consequences. Late filing of statutory forms may attract prescribed additional fees, while serious or fraudulent violations can lead to further penalties or prosecution under applicable provisions of the LLP Act.
